title: The one road you cannot lose
hook: Close any one road. Which closures actually cut the map in two?

knows: depth-first search visits every town it can reach (maze-depth-first)
a map of towns and roads is a graph
doesNotKnow: that some single roads are critical (bridges) and others are not
how to tell which ones they are

misconception: The busiest town's roads are the weak points, and closing almost any road matters.
objective: The learner can explain that a road is a bridge exactly when it lies on no loop, so in the map made of triangle 1-2-3, road 3-4 and triangle 4-5-6 only closing 3-4 splits the network, and that depth-first search can find all bridges in one pass.

claims.text: On this map (triangle 1-2-3, road 3-4, triangle 4-5-6), closing 3-4 cuts towns 4, 5 and 6 off from 1, 2 and 3; closing any of the other six roads leaves every town reachable.
claims.source: Demo.tsx reach() flood-fills from town 1 with each road removed, the same code the stage uses; builder re-ran it in a separate node script (scratchpad algo2b0/check.mjs), 2026-10-14: only 3-4 leaves 3 of 6 towns reachable. Matches brief cs.algorithms #76. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Re-ran Demo.tsx reach() for each road: only 3-4 leaves {1,2,3}; others reach all 6.

claims.text: Towns 3 and 4 each touch three roads, yet closing the triangle roads beside them changes nothing.
claims.source: Degree count from Demo.tsx ROADS (town 3: 2-3, 1-3, 3-4; town 4: 3-4, 4-5, 4-6); flood-fill result as in c1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Degrees from ROADS: town 3 = 3, town 4 = 3; closing 2-3, 1-3, 4-5, 4-6 keeps all 6.

claims.text: A road on a loop has a detour; a bridge is a road on no loop, so it has none.
claims.source: If edge u-v lies on a cycle, the rest of the cycle is a u..v path without it, so removing it disconnects nothing. If removing u-v leaves a u..v path, that path plus u-v is a cycle. CLRS 4e ch. 20 problem 20-2 (articulation points, bridges and biconnected components). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Cycle/detour equivalence re-derived (both directions).

claims.text: Depth-first search finds every bridge in one pass by noting, for each road it walks down, whether the towns below can climb back above it by another road.
claims.source: Tarjan (1974), 'A note on finding the bridges of a graph', Information Processing Letters 2(6); low-link values: tree edge (u, v) is a bridge iff low[v] > disc[u]. CLRS 4e ch. 20, problem 20-2. Runs in linear time O(V + E). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Implemented low-link DFS (bridge iff low[v] > disc[u]) on this map: returns only 3-4. Tarjan (1974) IPL 2(6) and CLRS 4e problem 20-2 cited from memory, not opened; the description matches the standard algorithm.

claims.text: Coloured towns can still be reached from town 1; red towns are cut off.
claims.source: Stage convention: Demo.tsx colours towns in reach(closed) with var(--domain), others var(--bad). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Demo.tsx fills reach(closed) towns var(--domain), others var(--bad).

recall.question: A network road lies on a loop of three towns. If that road is closed, what happens?
options: Nothing is cut off: traffic goes the other way round the loop
The two towns it joined are cut off from each other
It depends on how busy its towns are
recall.why: A road on a loop always has a detour, the rest of the loop. Only a bridge, a road on no loop, splits the network when closed.
